"LeBlanc dead," I said. "Ult, forty."

"Baron's resetting," Sana said. "They're backing off the pit — they've lost the damage, they can't do it now. But Vex—"

"I know," I said.

The third wave was in the base.

I could see it on the minimap the way you see the bill on the counter: four super minions and a cannon and a train of casters walking into our open top lane, our nexus turret with its little health bar getting smaller.

"Draven's still up," Sana said. "He's greedy, he's going to follow—"

Draven followed. Of course he did. Draven has never in his life said no to a fight, and he came around the back of the river mouth with his axes spinning, and my ult was at thirty-one.

Thirty. Twenty-nine.

"Kade, hold him," I said. "Hold him for nineteen."

"I'm holding!" Kade shouted, which is what Kade says when he's about to die. He Ghosted into Draven's face and ate the axes and did not die, because Darius at twenty-nine minutes has a health bar like a filing cabinet.

The ult came up. "Rengar ult, up."

I went. Grey, quiet, Q, Q, Profane — and Draven's health bar left like it had somewhere better to be, and his axes fell on the floor of the river and stopped spinning.

"Draven dead," I said. "Ult, forty. Go home. Go home now."

We ran.

That's the part nobody puts in the highlight reel — four people sprinting down the river with a super wave eating their base, boots and Ghost and Sana's ball pinging ahead of us. Baron reset behind us. We hadn't taken it. We'd only stopped them taking it, which is a different and worse thing, but it was the only thing we could afford.

We hit the choke at 30:10.

The wave was already inside. Four super minions shoulder to shoulder, the cannon behind them, casters flooding the gap where the inhibitor used to be. And Kade did the only thing Kade is truly good for: he walked into it. He walked into four super minions and let them hit him, and his health bar went down like a countdown, and he shouted, "I'm tanking! I'm tanking! Somebody do something!"

"Ball on the back line," Sana said, and dragged the casters into the wall, where they turned like dogs at a whistle.

"Lantern the cannon," Ilya said. "Or don't. I'll die either way." He lanterned Kade out of the middle of the wave, hooked the front super minion off Bo's face, and said nothing else about it.

Bo counted. "Two-ten. Two-eleven. Two-twelve." Each number a small prayer. He shot the cannon and the cannon came apart and the wave started to fold in on itself.

I ran the edge with my ult at thirty-eight. Full-damage Rengar does not tank waves. I threw Q into a caster, took a third of my health, backed into the fog, and waited like a man waiting for a bus he knows is late.

The wave broke at 30:40. All of it. The huge ones, the little ones, the whole terrible family — and then there was just the floor of our base and the four of us breathing, and Kade at a hundred and forty health saying, "See? See? I tanked it. I'm the tank."

"You're a wall with a mouth," Ilya said.

"Push," Sana said. "They're all dead or recalling. First time all game we can push. Bot inhibitor — go bot, it's the closest, it's the only one not behind two turrets."

We pushed out. That was the strange part, walking out of our base instead of into it. The map opened like a hand unclenching. Kade went to push the top wave because of course he did, and then actually turned around when I shouted, and we went bot as five.

The enemy bot inhibitor came down at 31:20 like a fence post. Bo hit it, Kade hit it, I hit it, and it fell, and the sound it made was the best sound in the game.

"First inhibitor," Sana said. "Ours, I mean. Our first. They respawn in ten. Baron's up in thirty."

"Second inhibitor," I said. "Mid. That's the real one. Take mid and the nexus turrets open up and then it's just a race we can actually win."

"Backdoor," Ilya said, in his flat doom voice, and for once it didn't sound like doom at all. "The boy wants to backdoor. Of course he does. Nobody follows him."

"Nobody follows me," I said, and my ult started counting.

# Two Marks in the Rain

Rain made the route board look newly painted. The red closure line was older than the rain, however, and Rafi could see where somebody had traced it twice to prevent travellers calling the first stroke ambiguous. Beyond the shelter, the lower path ran beneath a wall of water spilling from the hillside. He had guided people through worse weather on other routes. That experience gave him no right to pretend this route was open. He put his pack under the roof and waited for Jun to finish reading the board herself.

The route board confirmed that the lower path was closed for the night. Rafi read the closure board and knew the lower path was closed for the night. Jun asked whether closed meant impassable or forbidden. He said it meant they would not test the difference in darkness. Eamon, their porter, set down the food sack and began looking for a place where water would not drip into the fastening. They had enough daylight to make a camp and not enough to turn impatience into a sensible route decision.

Eamon was alive and mending the shoulder strap beside the shelter door. He used a bent needle which he kept in a cork, and complained that every borrowed sack had been designed for a person with another arrangement of shoulders. Rafi offered to exchange loads tomorrow. Eamon said tomorrow was the correct time to make such an offer, since tonight he intended to eat without having to admire Rafi's generosity. Jun laughed and then checked the drying line, making a small task out of giving them room to be familiar with each other.

The team used two litres for supper, reducing its measured water from twenty litres to eighteen. Rafi measured it from the graduated containers before heating the food. They had collected no additional water that evening. “We have eighteen litres left,” Jun said after reading the graduated containers. The figures mattered because the next day's route might take them away from the river for several hours. Eamon asked whether the rain could be persuaded to enter a container instead of his collar. Jun set an empty pan beneath the roof edge, but they did not count its contents before there were any.

The canoe rested on its rack beside the lower river shelter. They had first set it by the door to unload, then carried it under the overhanging roof and raised it onto the rack. Both positions belonged to the same shelter site. The short move protected the hull and cleared the doorway; it did not mean that somebody had secretly taken the canoe upriver. Rafi wrote SHELTER beside its location on the equipment sheet, a broad description intended to help another guide find the camp rather than reproduce the exact angle of its bow.

A loose stone struck Rafi’s right shin and left a spreading bruise. It had rolled when he tested the rack's rear support with his boot. He stopped, waited for the first sharp ache to settle and checked that the leg would bear him. Eamon suggested that the canoe could inspect the rest of the rack for itself. Rafi moved the loose stone away instead. A small injury was not an omen about the whole expedition, although he knew how easily a tired group could begin treating each inconvenience as evidence that a journey had chosen against them.

The expedition register named Jun as the apprentice navigator. She read the title when she signed the day's movement sheet, neither hiding it nor apologising for it. Rafi had asked for an apprentice because the route needed more than one person able to read it. He discovered that he had nevertheless arranged the map, the bearing notes and the route book on his own side of the shelter. Inviting someone to learn was not the same as letting her do the part that would teach her anything.

Rafi passed the route book to Jun, who sealed it inside a transparent dry bag. Before she sealed it, Eamon held it for a moment to read the shelter number and passed it back without tearing, marking or removing any page. Preserving the book did not require banning a companion from consulting it. Jun kept the bag open long enough for Rafi to identify the current route sheet, then closed the fastening in front of him. The cover was worn, but its condition was the same as when they had taken it from the depot.

Rafi initially held the mistaken belief that Jun had never handled this route book. He began explaining the awkward fastening in a voice he used with first-time visitors. Jun showed her signed depot check in the book, correcting Rafi’s mistaken assumption. She had inspected the pages during training and knew which corner of the sleeve caught the cover. He stopped halfway through his explanation. It was uncomfortable to discover that his careful instruction had been based on a fact he had never checked.

“Show me what you marked,” he said.

She showed him the training tabs, each labelled with a route rather than a conclusion. Rafi invited Jun to mark the first bearing, then checked it with her rather than replacing it. Jun believed she could navigate the high route under supervision, but had not yet attempted it. She did not claim that reading a map in the depot had already given her the experience of moving across the ridge. Rafi found her careful confidence easier to trust once he stopped expecting it to resemble his own manner of speaking.

Beyond the marked turn stood a second cairn with a flat black stone, absent from the current route sheet. They could see it through a break in the rain from the shelter's raised floor. The first cairn carried a painted arrow corresponding to the board. The second had no paint. Eamon suspected the second cairn marked an older route; the stones alone did not establish its age. He had seen it on previous journeys and had never needed to ask where it led. Necessity did not create an answer merely by arriving late.

A red thread crossed the old route-book stitch, and no entry explained who had repaired it. Jun noticed it while comparing the sheet number with the register. The thread was tight enough to hold, and the visible pages were complete according to the current index. Rafi could not remember whether it had been there when he first borrowed the book. He did not say that it had appeared overnight. A thing newly noticed could be old, and the route already contained enough uncertainty without assigning every unfamiliar detail a recent origin.

A two-note whistle sounded from upriver after dark, with no visible boat to answer it. Eamon raised his head, waiting for an engine. None followed. The whistle could have come from a person or a bird; the sound did not identify its source. Jun listened for a repetition and heard only rain against the roof. Rafi marked the time on the movement sheet. A remembered sound might be useful later, provided he did not attach a person or a destination to it while the hillside was still hiding both.

“The north landing has washed away,” Eamon said, repeating a traveller’s report without seeing the landing himself. Rafi asked when the traveller had last visited it. Eamon did not know. The report concerned a real place and might be important, but its date and source were missing. If the north landing were gone, they would have to wait for the relief boat; its condition was still unknown. They put that possibility beside the high-route question instead of altering the destination column as though they had inspected the damage.

The river gate moves only when its hand capstan is turned; the intact gate has no motor, remote control or automatic release. Rafi explained this while pointing out the capstan symbol on the map. Opening the gate could change the level in a narrow side channel, but it was not something the river did by itself when travellers needed a favour. Jun traced the path to the inspection point with her finger. She asked whether they should send someone now. Rafi looked at the fading light and said the inspection belonged to morning.

Years before this expedition, Rafi had waited at the north landing for a boat that never came. He remembered a dry coat becoming damp while he checked the same empty bend, and the ridiculous anger he felt at the water for continuing to move. The failure had taught him to request a clear collection time. It had not taught him the landing's condition tonight. Eamon asked whether that old boat had ever been found. Rafi said he had found the booking error instead. Sometimes a failed journey had an ordinary explanation which became visible only after a miserable wait.

At dawn, Rafi intended to inspect the gate before choosing a route; he made no inspection that night. He wrote the intention under TOMORROW so it would not be confused with a completed visit. Eamon finished the strap and hung the needle's cork on the food sack. Jun checked the bag around the route book one more time, then placed it beside her folded coat. The work of stopping looked modest from outside: warm food, a dry fastening and a question left unanswered until there was light to investigate it.

Rafi stayed at the lower river shelter after the rain closed the path. In the quiet between showers he could hear Eamon breathe through a blocked nose and Jun turn once in her sleeping bag. Jun dreamed of a dry river carrying their canoe through the air, then woke beside the wet containers. She told him about the dream with a tired smile. Outside, the canoe remained on its rack, the lower route remained closed, and the second cairn waited beyond the painted turn with no explanation of its own.

# Above the Flood Line

By morning the rain had become a finer thing, less visible and no less persistent. Rafi's first steps made the bruise in his shin feel larger than the leg around it. He did not announce this as a difficulty for the group. He asked Jun to lead the short walk to the gate inspection point while he followed closely enough to check the path. Eamon carried the repaired sack without remarking on the new strap. The shelter looked smaller behind them, which made leaving it feel more definite than the mark Rafi had put on the movement sheet.

The gate's capstan stood beneath a lean roof beyond the bend. Its hand grips were wet and motionless. They inspected the approach from the safe marked path and found no sign of a recent opening. Rafi did not turn it: the closure board concerned the flooded lower path, and they had no instruction authorising a change to the gate. Yesterday's intention to inspect had now become an actual visit. The choice of route still had to follow the visit rather than masquerade as something the map had already decided for them.

Jun suggested examining the gap near the second cairn before committing the loads to it. Rafi thought the gap ended against a rock wall. He could not remember having looked beyond the wall, which was a poor foundation for the confidence with which he had described it. Eamon offered to stay with the canoe while they checked. Rafi accepted, and noticed the relief of allowing a decision to be provisional without making it directionless. They could test the route in daylight and return if the way ahead failed to match the sheet.

Jun found an old cut arrow beneath the second cairn’s black stone, pointing towards the high traverse. She moved only a loose twig to make it visible, leaving the cairn itself intact. The old cut arrow suggested an intended route, but did not reveal who had cut it or when. Jun compared its bearing with the ridge on the map and asked to check the first visible section. Rafi followed her to a position from which he could see the return path. The arrow made a useful question more specific. It did not certify the next mile.

Rafi had wrongly believed the second cairn led only to a dead end before Jun tested the marked gap. Rafi watched Jun emerge along the high traverse and saw his dead-end belief disproved. She had found the path returning around the rock shoulder at a higher level. Jun’s completed traverse established that the high route was passable that day. That was what her actual movement established: a route available under present conditions, not a guarantee about every season or every traveller who might later attempt it.

Rafi appointed Jun acting route leader for the exposed traverse. She checked where the loads could pass and where the canoe would need a line. Rafi followed Jun’s chosen bearing without taking the route book back to overrule her. Eamon watched the two of them from the waiting place and called that it was pleasant to see a map being used from both sides. Rafi wanted to answer with a joke, but was concentrating on the narrow path. He raised one hand instead, the ordinary gesture becoming significant only after the day was over.

Jun put the route book into Rafi’s dry bag before climbing the last step. She needed both hands free to check the line position. Its temporary passage through Eamon's hands while they moved the bag changed neither its contents nor the final handover to Rafi. Rafi checked the fastening when she was clear of the step. The book stayed dry and complete. No one needed to make possession permanent merely to prove that they understood why the pages mattered to the next team.

They hauled the canoe onto the high granite ledge with the hand line. The movement took longer than Rafi expected because they stopped to adjust the hull twice rather than force it against the rock. There was room to set it level and enough shelter to wait before the next exposed stretch. Rafi’s bruised right shin was stiff, but he could put his weight on that leg. He moved slowly when he helped lift the bow. Being able to bear weight did not mean the bruise had disappeared, and he told Jun which part of the load he could safely take.

They collected five litres of rainwater and then used two, taking the measured supply from eighteen litres to twenty-one. Jun poured the collection into the graduated containers before measuring the cooking water out. Eamon checked the new figures while Rafi dealt with the line. “Twenty-one litres, including what we collected,” Rafi said, checking each container. The supply had increased despite their drinking and cooking because they had added more than they used. Jun kept both entries on the sheet instead of compressing the account into a single unexplained number.

A numbered depot stamp crossed the red thread, connecting the repair to an old inventory but naming no repairer. Rafi had opened the book under the shelter of the upturned canoe to check the next route number. Jun compared the stamp with the current depot label and found a different series. Jun suspected the repaired stitch marked a removed leaf, but no torn edge proved it. The indexed pages were still present. They could investigate an old repair without reporting that a specific page had been lost when they had not found a gap.

Rafi listened for the sound of an engine and heard water against stone. He did not tell her that the explanation was impossible. He told her they lacked the observation needed to make it certain. It was a small exchange, interrupted before either of them imagined they would remember the day chiefly for something else.

The rock strike came from the slope above the waiting place. Rafi heard the first impact, turned, and saw Eamon fall beside the food sack. There was no heroic interval in which the sound explained itself slowly enough for everyone to choose a different movement. Jun reached him first. Rafi put the line down and joined her. For a time their world became the space beside Eamon, the urgent calls they made to him and the desperate hope that an ordinary breath would answer those calls. No answer came that would make their effort sufficient.

Eamon died on the ledge after the rock strike; Rafi and Jun witnessed his final breath and could not revive him. Jun witnessed Eamon’s final breath and knew he had died. Rafi had no sentence which could turn that knowledge into something gentler. He covered Eamon and sat beside the body until Jun asked what they should do next. The question was not cold. It was the only way she could keep the rest of the day from dissolving. He answered the part he could answer and did not offer a promise about the part he could not.

They moved the waiting equipment away from the loose slope and secured the covered body on the broadest part of the ledge. The recovery would require another team and different equipment. Rafi recorded the location carefully, with marks another person could recognise. He did not attempt to make an unsafe descent carrying a burden they could not control. Eamon had carried enough burdens for them while alive. Treating grief as an instruction to create another casualty would have honoured neither his work nor his habitual, unsentimental care for other people.

Rafi briefly imagined Eamon adjusting the load behind him, then recognised the image as grief, not a living companion. He told Jun when his attention slipped. She checked the line again without demanding that he conceal it. Their remaining responsibilities were smaller than what had happened, but they remained real.

Rafi remembered the same unanswered wait at the north landing years ago; it was not where he stood now. He had thought of that old experience yesterday as a story about an inconvenience. They had no working signal there. Writing the intended call on the movement sheet did not make it transmitted or guarantee that anybody below would expect it.

Rafi believed Jun could lead the remaining traverse, based on the route she had just completed. He told her to choose where they would stop for the night and to wake him if she wanted a second reading of the map. Jun asked whether acting leader meant she should stop asking questions. He said it meant she should decide which questions needed another person's view. It was the best answer he could make without pretending that a title protected anyone from uncertainty. She opened the map and began by naming the next visible landmark.

The canoe was secure, the route book dry, and the measured water supply sufficient. These facts mattered without balancing the other fact. Jun placed Eamon's repaired sack beside the covered body and left the needle in its cork. Beyond the bend the whistle did not sound again. They would carry its question forward, together with a route somebody else would need and a name they would have to say when they reached the landing.

A six-pound entry rebate increased the travel fund from eighty-four pounds to ninety. The registrar returned the money because the programme had incorrectly charged their reserve entry twice. She wanted a number they could understand without remembering why the first envelope had been thin.

Nessa asked to practise one more exchange before the change. Ada said yes before remembering that saying yes was supposed to cost her something. It cost only another run along the same short stretch of track.

It was the first story about him she had told without using it to measure somebody else.

Ada stayed at the municipal relay track after the afternoon exchange trials. Her palm ached, her legs shook, and the card was no longer in her pocket. None of those facts meant the day had gone wrong. Across the painted line, Nessa was waiting for her to choose where they would practise next.

# A Plinth with No Object

On Monday morning Leila found the pedestal wearing a paper hat. The hat was an accident, a folded delivery sheet which had slid off a crate and settled on the empty display surface. She took it off before the director arrived. The exhibition had already been described as playful in three separate grant applications, and she did not want anyone deciding that this meant objects could organise themselves. She needed a clear floor, a matching delivery register and a temporary assistant who would answer to his own name.

Tom arrived wearing a badge that said TORN. The replacement badge printer had mistaken the corner of an old label for part of the lettering. He apologised as if the error reflected a difficult family history. Leila said they could repair it later. She was carrying three versions of the morning briefing, none of which explained why the display pedestal had arrived before the object it was meant to support. The packing list did not call the object missing. It left the object column entirely blank.

Tom’s badge identified him as the temporary stage assistant. Beneath the damaged name, the job title had printed correctly. He read it whenever someone asked him a question, apparently checking whether the answer belonged to him. Leila gave him a tour of the exhibition workshop, including the recessed bench behind the folding screen. The bench was inside the workshop, although staff called it the back office when they wanted to eat lunch without interruption. Tom wrote both names in his folder and drew an arrow between them.

An eight-pound tape purchase reduced petty cash from seventy-two pounds to sixty-four. Leila had bought the wide tape because the cheaper roll left a pale stripe on the floor. Nobody had authorised the wider tape as a distinct financial category, so she wrote down its use rather than inventing one. Bev was alive and arguing cheerfully with the adding machine. Its paper output curled across her wrist like a long accusation. “There are sixty-four pounds in the tin,” Bev said after making two neat piles. The machine, for once, agreed with her.

Leila offered Bev the delivery slip to inspect against the cashbook reference. Bev held it under her lamp, read the supplier number and returned it with all its corners and writing intact. The slip was required to survive the exhibition, which did not prevent the accounts clerk from reading it. Leila gave the delivery slip to Tom, who put it in his folder. Tom asked whether he should now guard the folder. Leila said he should bring it when somebody needed the delivery information. He looked relieved to have a job involving movement.

“The mayor has already cancelled the exhibition,” Tom said, quoting a message from an anonymous account. Bev asked which mayor, which exhibition and which account. Tom had answers only to the middle question. The director arrived at that moment carrying a box of invitations for the rehearsal and asked them to check the postage. No cancellation had been issued. Tom crossed a line through his note, then apologised for having a phone. Bev suggested apologising for trusting it would be a more practical start.

The delivery register marked the pedestal unchecked, not missing. Leila read UNCHECKED in the register and knew it was not a missing-object report. Checking meant measuring the delivered structure, confirming the surface finish and signing beside the correct supplier number. None of those tasks required knowing the shape of the eventual exhibit. The director explained this twice, then admitted she did not know what the eventual exhibit would be either. It was arriving separately under a loan arrangement administered by an office which answered questions only on Thursdays.

The empty pedestal stood in the exhibition workshop. It was wider than Leila expected and sat on four lockable castors, two of which disagreed about the direction in which wheels ought to move. Three spare screws lay taped beneath the pedestal, with no visible sockets to receive them. Tom discovered them while trying to find the castor lock. He placed them on a clean cloth and counted them so solemnly that Bev asked whether they had joined the payroll. He put them back under the tape without taking the joke as an instruction.

The empty object label carried a blue dot that appeared on no public catalogue. Leila compared three printed lists before deciding that a fourth comparison would merely prove her persistence. The dot was not a name. It did not identify an artist, an insurer or a date. The dot might have been a packing code, but the unsigned label did not establish that. She photographed it for the regional office and drafted a question which did not contain the word urgent. Adding that word to every message had made it function like a greeting.

A small bell rang inside the sealed delivery crate whenever it tilted, though the packing list named no bell. Tom tilted it twice to demonstrate the effect, then stopped when Leila asked whether a third demonstration would teach them anything new. The box carried instructions to keep it closed until the public unpacking. Its straps were intact. Bev suggested leaving it level, since this both respected the instructions and stopped the sound. Leila recorded that suggestion as the first exhibition decision made without requiring another form.

The intact receipt machine prints only on its numbered paper roll; with the roll removed it cannot produce a paper receipt. Bev showed Tom how to check the roll before trying to print a supplier acknowledgement. It was a plain mechanical limitation rather than an opinion from accounts. She removed the roll, pressed the lever to demonstrate an empty movement and put the paper back. No receipt appeared while it was absent. Tom said the machine would make an excellent model for the regional office, which also performed movements without issuing answers.

Leila initially misbelieved Tom had ignored the briefing because he kept consulting his folder. She asked him to put it down while she explained the handling route. His hands tightened on the cover. When Tom unfolded the badge backing, Leila saw the briefing instructions printed underneath it. He had been checking a tiny copy of the instructions which the replacement badge had concealed. Leila read enough to recognise her own badly chosen phrase about fluid operational boundaries. She told him that keeping the instructions was sensible, and that she would print a copy a person could read without undressing a badge.

Leila agreed to work beside Tom instead of sending him away for another badge. They measured the pedestal together, one holding the tape while the other tried to find the beginning of the number scale. Tom had brought his own small square, which fitted the corner more neatly than the exhibition ruler. He did not make a speech about having it. Leila noticed that she had been treating his uncertainty as evidence against his competence when it might simply mean he was willing to ask where an unfamiliar thing belonged.

A stiff shoe raised a small blister on Leila’s right heel. She sat on the recessed bench behind the workshop screen and took the shoe off. From there she could still see the pedestal through the gap where the screen failed to meet the wall. She remained inside the workshop throughout the pause. Bev supplied a pad from the first-aid box, together with an account of the last coordinator who had tried to organise an exhibition in new shoes. That coordinator had apparently blamed the floor.

Long before this exhibition, Leila had slept in the civic gallery during a student installation. She remembered waking under a table while a tutor explained that an audience was always part of the work. At the time she had interpreted that as an artistic principle. Now she thought it might also have been advice about having chairs ready. Tom believed the exhibition would expose his inexperience, although nobody had criticised his work. Leila recognised the expression on his face because she had once mistaken being new for having committed an error.

Bev suspected the three spare screws belonged to an attachment, but had not seen that attachment. She made a little sketch instead of entering a lost-part claim. Leila approved the distinction. A piece without an obvious home was a question; it became a loss only when they knew what was absent. The empty label and the bell remained questions too. She collected them on a single page where they could wait without acquiring answers from the pressure of being inconvenient.

Tom intended to call the mayor after lunch, but had not dialled the number. Leila asked him to postpone it until the director checked the anonymous message. If the crate held a live performer, the bell might be a signal; nobody opened it on that assumption. Tom suggested this explanation with an expression which made it difficult to tell whether he was joking. Bev said that a performer with a bell should have insisted on a better contract. They left the straps alone and returned to measuring the pedestal.

By the end of the briefing, Tom had a corrected badge, a legible instruction sheet and a folder containing an intact delivery slip. Leila stayed in the exhibition workshop after the morning briefing. She closed her eyes on the bench while the kettle warmed. In a brief doze Leila dreamed that the pedestal delivered a speech, then woke to Tom’s real voice. He was asking where to put the empty cups. The pedestal had said nothing, but for the first time that morning Leila could answer a question without needing somebody in another building to return a call.

Leila had been right-handed from birth and had never been left-handed.

With no intervening gain or loss after that completed count, the very same balance was 71 pounds, not 64 pounds.

# An Audience for the Wrapping

On Wednesday the director announced that they would rehearse the public unpacking before they had permission to unpack anything. She had found an empty box with the right proportions, a secondhand length of ribbon and a lectern from the committee room. Tom asked whether the substitute box needed a substitute packing list. Leila said no, then reconsidered when the director began discussing where the imaginary screws would go. Bev supplied a sheet marked REHEARSAL in letters large enough to protect the accounts from artistic interpretation.

The civic gallery was long enough for a procession and narrow enough to make a procession seem inevitable. The pedestal had to turn between two columns before reaching its display space. Tom wheeled the pedestal into the civic gallery and locked its castors. He tested each lock by pushing from a different side. Leila noticed the extra care, remembered her first judgement of him and let him finish without offering a correction. The floor would be full of visitors on Saturday. Taking a minute to discover which wheel moved was better than discovering it with a visitor attached.

A ten-pound deposit refund increased petty cash from sixty-four pounds to seventy-four. The supplier had returned the charge for a missing tape dispenser after finding the dispenser in its own van. Bev counted the refund into the existing fund before writing the new total. “The fund is seventy-four pounds now,” Bev said, matching the refund to the cash. Leila checked the sequence: the original purchase had reduced the fund, and the later refund increased it. The larger balance did not contradict the smaller balance from Monday. Between them stood an actual ten-pound return.

A fresh pad protected the healing blister on Leila’s right heel; it had not vanished. She changed into the soft shoes she kept beneath the gallery desk. By the time she followed Tom between the columns, her steps no longer had Monday's careful unevenness. This was an improvement in comfort, not proof that she had fabricated the injury. She could still feel the blister if she pressed the back of her shoe against it. She stopped doing so because checking the existence of discomfort did not make an event easier to organise.

The director appointed Tom acting stage manager for the afternoon rehearsal. She gave him a clipboard which had belonged to so many predecessors that its elastic band was mostly knot. The director told Tom he was acting stage manager for that rehearsal only. He repeated the limit back to her. Leila liked this more than she would have liked a ceremonial declaration of leadership. Somebody needed to call the sequence. Giving that responsibility a clear beginning and end let the rest of them follow it without inventing a dispute over rank.

Tom handed the delivery slip to Bev for the reconciliation. She spread it beside the supplier's confirmation and asked Leila to verify the dimensions. Bev signed the delivery register after checking that the pedestal was intact. The slip itself remained uncut and unaltered. Reading and signing the separate register did not damage the document that would eventually return to Leila. Tom watched the process once, then returned to the rehearsal marks. He had learned the difference between safeguarding a thing and preventing anyone from using it.

Leila removed the numbered paper roll and gave it to Bev to count. The receipt machine stayed on the gallery desk with its compartment open. For the rehearsal, Tom used a blank card labelled SAMPLE instead of asking the empty machine for a printed acknowledgement. Bev counted the unused paper at a side table. The actual machine produced nothing while its roll was away. They were preparing to show how a delivery worked, not pretending that a demonstration changed the mechanics of the equipment.

“The blue dot means the object is radioactive,” Tom joked, and immediately said he was inventing that. The director asked whether he would use that line with the visitors. He said he would not. Leila could see that the joke was an attempt to make uncertainty less frightening, but an audience would have no reason to know which parts of his account were invented. They agreed to say exactly what they knew about the dot: it was on the label, and its meaning had not yet been confirmed.

A private loan form repeated the blue dot beside an unnamed regional depot. Leila had found the form in an attachment beneath the supplier's latest message. The form explained which office had sent the crate but not which building the office meant by depot. It moved the question one step without finishing it. Bev suspected the bell belonged to reusable packaging rather than the missing artwork. The straps and reusable corner guards made that plausible, but a plausible explanation did not need to enter the object record as an established fact.

The unexplained bell sounded again when they tilted the sealed crate for the rehearsal. They had placed it on a separate trolley, still closed, to practise the route without opening it. Tom stopped the trolley when he heard the bell, checked that the straps held and began again more slowly. A guard passing the door asked whether the exhibition had started. Bev said that if rehearsal noises counted, they had been open since Monday. The guard stayed long enough to watch them negotiate the second column, then offered to hold a door on Saturday.

The workshop diagram showed three holes beneath a removable reading shelf, but the shelf was not in the crate. Leila had found the drawing inside the pedestal's maintenance envelope. It made the three loose screws more intelligible without locating the actual shelf. The director remembered authorising a separate shipment of flat fittings. Her memory was useful enough to pursue, not enough to sign for a delivery which nobody had seen. Tom wrote SHELF on the questions page and left the status beside it blank.

Leila believed a plain explanation would work better than another apology, but the audience had not yet arrived. They practised a short opening that acknowledged a staggered delivery and described what visitors would actually see. The director wanted to call the empty space an invitation to imagine. Leila suggested saying that the object would be installed after its condition check. Tom tried both versions, and everyone agreed that the second gave an audience a better chance of understanding why a box was still shut.

Tom briefly believed, wrongly, that the audience had been told the empty pedestal was the exhibit. He had seen a cropped photograph from the publicity office and assumed it was the complete invitation. The invitation corrected Tom’s mistake: it advertised a demonstration of unpacking, not an empty-pedestal artwork. Leila let him read the whole paragraph before explaining the schedule. A mistaken interpretation was easier to revise when nobody treated its correction as a public punishment. He placed the invitation on top of his clipboard, where it could compete fairly with the photograph.

Leila let Tom lead the rehearsal and stood ready to answer only when he asked. His first introduction was too fast. On the second attempt he looked at the room rather than at the director. On the third he remembered to leave a space for people to move between the columns. He did not become a different person between attempts. He acquired a sequence of actions he could trust. Leila realised she had spent much of Monday wanting an assistant who already knew her unspoken procedures, which was a demanding qualification for temporary employment.

Leila recalled the same student night in the gallery; recalling it did not put her back in that earlier year. From the desk she could see the table beneath which she had slept, now supporting a stack of folded chairs. She wondered whether the tutor would have approved their plain introduction. It did not matter enough to ask anyone to guess. The audience on Saturday would need room to stand and an explanation of the actual delivery. A remembered teacher was entitled to remain a memory instead of chairing another meeting.

Bev planned to refund the ticket deposits tomorrow; no ticket refund was made that afternoon. She wanted the demonstration list checked first so the wrong visitor would not receive somebody else's money. If the audience refused the demonstration, they would need a new programme; the audience had not voted. Tom wrote this possible problem on a separate sheet rather than announcing a cancellation. Leila thanked him for keeping future contingencies away from the list of things that had already gone wrong.

Tom described a dream in which the mayor arrived disguised as a pedestal; nobody treated it as a visit. The director asked whether the mayor had spoken better in the dream. Bev said they ought not charge a dream appearance fee without a numbered receipt. The joke lasted exactly long enough to let them restart the rehearsal without resentment. A muffled sound from the corridor could have been the mayor’s laugh, but no one saw who made it. They did not add a mayoral attendance to the programme on that evidence.

After the public rehearsal, which involved the staff and two willing guards rather than ticket holders, Tom stacked the spare chairs and returned the clipboard. Leila remained in the civic gallery after the public rehearsal. The pedestal stood secure on its locked wheels. The real crate stayed strapped and level. Bev still held the counted paper roll, and the receipt machine remained silent on the desk. There were fewer answers than Leila had wanted on Monday, but the questions had stopped disguising themselves as failures. Saturday could now be approached as a sequence of tasks rather than a single enormous thing called opening.

While its paper roll was removed and no other paper was supplied, the intact receipt machine printed a new paper receipt.

Tom died permanently at that moment, and the death was confirmed before the chapter ended.
